strengths: The core idea is clean, conceptually appealing, and practically useful: freezing the base model and training only a lightweight adapter (often as simple as a scalar affine map with d + 1 parameters) allows models to self-interpret internal representations without risking distortion of internal computations through model fine-tuning.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple model families (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen-2.5 7B-72B, Gemma-2-9B) and varied tasks (SAE latent interpretation, contrastive topic retrieval, and multi-hop reasoning implicit entity decoding).

High-quality ablation and diagnostic studies that thoroughly unpack what the adapter learns (e.g., PCA analysis explaining why full-rank overfits SAE features but succeeds on contrastive vectors, ALL-CAPS label manipulation showing the separation of format in the bias vs. semantics in the activation, and zero-vector probing).

The demonstration that cross-layer adapters match or outperform layer-specific adapters is a striking finding that illuminates the geometric consistency of semantic representations across transformer layers.

The application to multi-hop implicit reasoning ('catching models red-handed') demonstrates clear utility for alignment auditing, extracting unverbalized intermediate entities significantly more reliably than untrained baselines.
weaknesses: The paper lacks direct quantitative benchmarking against concurrent decoder fine-tuning approaches (such as LatentQA or Activation Oracles / Li et al., 2025). While the paper convincingly argues conceptually why freezing the model is preferable for preserving privileged access, an empirical trade-off analysis (e.g., parameter count/compute vs. explanation accuracy/faithfulness) would strengthen the positioning.

Evaluation still relies on an inference-time best-of-N scale grid search. While Section 3.4 and Appendix A.5 demonstrate improved scale tolerance compared to untrained SelfIE, eliminating the multi-scale inference requirement entirely remains an open issue.

Generation scoring relies on the same model generating contexts to activate its own latents, which can occasionally favor broad or generic labels that artificially trigger feature activations. Although this is standard in automated interpretability, reporting complementary human evaluation or more extensive detection scoring on natural corpora across all benchmarks would enhance confidence.

strengths: Compelling conceptual reframing: The paper cleverly turns mechanistic interpretability artifacts (SAE decoder vectors and contrastive activation vectors) into supervised training signals, rather than viewing them merely as descriptive end-products.

Preservation of model weights: In contrast to recent work that fine-tunes the target model (e.g., via LoRA) and risks altering underlying internal representations, this work completely freezes the base LLM and trains only an ultra-lightweight adapter, preserving true 'privileged access'.

Clean mechanistic and architectural insights: The systematic exploration across adapter architectures (from scale-only up to full-rank affine) clearly demonstrates that a minimal scalar affine adapter ($d_{model} + 1$ parameters) captures ~85% of performance gains. The zero-vector probing and ALL-CAPS experiments convincingly isolate the role of the bias vector as a distributional/formatting prior versus the input vector as a semantic director.

Thorough controlled analyses: The authors provide compelling explanations (supported by PCA and controlled label-count experiments) for why full-rank affine adapters succeed on contrastive topic vectors (low intrinsic dimensionality) but catastrophically overfit on SAE decoder vectors.

Extensive cross-model scaling and generalization: The methodology is thoroughly validated across multiple open-weight LLM families (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Gemma-2-9B, and Qwen-2.5 from 7B to 72B), confirming cross-layer transfer and demonstrating that self-interpretation capability scales faster than general capability bounds (the Taboo baseline).

Practical demonstration of decoding unverbalized reasoning: The multi-hop reasoning application (TwoHopFact) shows that adapters trained on monosemantic vectors generalize well enough to extract unstated bridge entities from polysemantic residual stream activations.
weaknesses: Persistence of scale-tuning dependence: Although trained adapters significantly broaden the range of viable scales compared to untrained SelfIE (Figure 4), the primary evaluations still depend on a best-of-6 multi-scale generation protocol. In fully unsupervised auditing settings without ground truth to score against, choosing an optimal inference scale remains an open practical hurdle.

Rigidity of the prompt template: The adapter is trained exclusively on a single fixed explanation-seeking template ('What is the meaning of...'). While Section 5 discusses extensions to conversational Q&A probing, the framework currently lacks the flexible, task-conditioned query capability demonstrated by decoder fine-tuning approaches like LatentQA.

Evaluation specifics of generation scoring: The generation scoring protocol depends on prompt-based generation of short synthetic conversations, which can introduce generative biases or false positives if latents activate broadly or spuriously on particular conversational styles.

strengths: Innovative reframing of interpretability artifacts: The paper re-envisions existing interpretability outputs (SAE decoder vectors and contrastive activation vectors) not as final analytical endpoints, but as rich supervisory signals to train models to interpret their own representations.

Remarkable parameter efficiency and architectural insights: The discovery that a scalar affine adapter with merely d_model + 1 parameters provides ~85% of the performance gain—while avoiding the catastrophic overfitting observed with full-rank transformations on high-dimensional SAE data—is clean, surprising, and well-substantiated by empirical ablations.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation and scaling analysis: The authors validate the method across multiple model families (Llama 3.1 8B, Llama 3.3 70B, Gemma 2 9B, and Qwen 2.5 7B–72B) across both generation and detection metrics. The 'Taboo' benchmark offers a sound control isolating self-interpretation capability from baseline knowledge capacity across scale.

Compelling downstream application: Demonstrating that adapters trained on monosemantic artifacts transfer to polysemantic hidden states in multi-hop reasoning (TwoHopFact) to surface latent bridge entities without chain-of-thought provides strong evidence for the practical utility of frozen self-interpretation.

Insightful mechanistic analysis of adapter components: The controlled ALL-CAPS experiment and zero-vector analyses (Appendices I and J) convincingly demonstrate the functional decomposition where the bias vector encodes the task prior/format while the scaled activation vector supplies semantic specificity.
weaknesses: Restricted to a single prompt template: The framework is evaluated almost entirely using a single explanation-seeking prompt ('What is the meaning of "TOKEN"?'). Unlike concurrent decoder fine-tuning approaches (e.g., LatentQA, Activation Oracles), it does not accommodate arbitrary conversational questions or multifaceted querying about internal activations.

Continued reliance on multi-scale search: Although the trained adapter widens the band of functional scales compared to untrained SelfIE (Figures 4 and 16), optimal evaluation still depends on an external grid search over N = 6 scale multipliers rather than completely automating or endogenizing scale calibration.

Modest absolute generation frequency for bridge entity extraction: In the TwoHopFact reasoning evaluation, although the adapter detects the intermediate entity in 91% of prompts, the raw fraction of matching generations across all sampled tokens is 4.26%, indicating that extraction can still be sparse and sensitive to sampling noise.

strengths: Elegantly simple and principled approach: freezing the base model completely and learning only a lightweight adapter ($d_{\text{model}} + 1$ or low-rank parameters) avoids altering the underlying internal representations, directly addressing the core conceptual limitation of fine-tuning methods like LoRA-based Activation Oracles.

Thorough and rigorous empirical evaluation across multiple model families (Llama 3.1 8B, Llama 3.3 70B, Gemma 2 9B, Qwen 2.5 7B–72B) and multiple representation geometries (contrastive vectors and SAE features), showing strong out-of-distribution transfer and favorable scaling behavior.

Insightful mechanistic analysis of adapter components: the paper clearly demonstrates that the learned bias vector acts as an 'interpretation prior' (substantiated by zero-vector probes and the clever ALL-CAPS experiment), and convincingly explains why full-rank adapters overfit on SAE features while succeeding on contrastive vectors through intrinsic dimensionality (PCA).

Compelling practical application to alignment auditing: successfully extracts unverbalized intermediate 'bridge entities' in multi-hop reasoning (TwoHopFact) without chain-of-thought, outperforming untrained baselines and competing favorably with linear probes.
Methodological honesty and rigor: the use of an independent two-phase select-and-rescore protocol explicitly prevents selection-on-noise artifacts in best-of-$N$ generation scoring.
weaknesses: Inference still relies on generating across multiple injection scales: the method requires evaluating a grid of scales ($N=6$) to achieve peak performance. In real-world auditing scenarios without ground-truth labels for candidate selection, determining the single best scale or candidate label remains an open challenge.

Restricted interaction format: unlike concurrent decoder-fine-tuning methods (e.g., LatentQA or Activation Oracles) that support flexible natural-language queries about activations, the adapter is tied to a single explanation-seeking soft-prompt template ('What is the meaning of TOKEN?').

Dependence on existing interpretability artifacts or synthetic supervision: training the adapters requires either large collections of auto-interpreted SAE vectors or contrastive vectors paired with synthetic descriptions (e.g., generated via Claude API).

strengths: Compelling and elegant conceptual framing: reframes existing interpretability artifacts (SAE decoder vectors, contrastive activation vectors) as supervision for self-interpretation, while keeping the base language model completely frozen to preserve the underlying representations.

Remarkably parsimonious architecture: demonstrates that a scalar affine transformation with just d_model + 1 parameters captures most of the performance gains (~85% of loss reduction attributable to the bias vector alone), avoiding catastrophic overfitting seen in high-capacity transformations on SAE latents.

Rigorous experimental methodology: includes a two-phase select-then-rescore evaluation protocol to eliminate selection-on-noise bias, clear comparisons against baselines (untrained SelfIE, paraphrases, LoRA activation oracles, linear probes), and well-controlled ablation experiments (e.g., isolating intrinsic dimensionality vs. label count).

Extensive cross-model and scaling analysis: evaluates multiple open-weight LLM families (Llama 3.1/3.3 8B and 70B, Gemma 2 9B, and Qwen 2.5 7B–72B), demonstrating that self-interpretation capability scales monotonically and outpaces capability improvements relative to a Taboo ceiling.

Impactful downstream demonstration: successfully extracts unverbalized intermediate reasoning entities in multi-hop question answering (TwoHopFact) without chain-of-thought, demonstrating generalization from monosemantic training to polysemantic runtime states.
weaknesses: Practical deployment requires scale sweeping: optimal generation relies on sampling across a grid of scales (N=6 candidates) and selecting via external scoring. In real-world exploratory interpretability workflows where ground-truth verification data is absent, selecting the optimal scale/candidate remains challenging.

Divergence between evaluation objectives: as detailed in Appendix K, detection-optimal and generation-optimal labels often diverge significantly across scale (preferring opposite ends of the scale grid), meaning the adapter does not yield a single unambiguous canonical interpretation for an activation vector without task-specific criteria.

Dependence on upstream synthetic/auto-interp quality: the training pipeline relies on LLM-generated synthetic labels or automated interpretability labels, which may carry systematic biases or lexical artifacts into the learned bias vector and adapter.

strengths: Compelling and parameter-efficient conceptual framework: By training only a lightweight affine transformation ($d_{model} + 1$ or low-rank parameters) while keeping the target LLM completely frozen, the approach preserves privileged self-access without the risk of distorting the model's underlying representations through weight fine-tuning.

Insightful mechanistic analysis of adapter components: The paper provides clear, elegant experiments explaining what the adapter learns—specifically showing that the bias vector acts as a task/format prior (demonstrated cleanly via zero-vector generation and the controlled ALL-CAPS experiment in Appendix I), while the activation vector governs instance-level semantics.

Comprehensive empirical validation across models and scales: Experiments evaluate multiple architectures and sizes (Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.3-70B, Gemma-2-9B, and Qwen-2.5 from 7B to 72B), testing both sparse autoencoder (SAE) decoder vectors and contrastive topic vectors.

Rigorous evaluation methodology: The authors design a principled two-phase selection-and-rescoring protocol (Appendix A.5) to avoid selection-on-noise bias in best-of-N candidate evaluations, and thoughtfully analyze the tension between detection-optimal and generation-optimal labels (Appendix K).

Promising auditing utility: The application to TwoHopFact multi-hop reasoning demonstrates practical value by recovering latent bridge entities that appear in neither the prompt nor the response, significantly outperforming untrained baselines and matching or exceeding linear probes.
weaknesses: Persistence of inference-time scale calibration: Although the adapter broadens the range of valid scales compared to untrained SelfIE, optimal decoding still relies on sweeping across a grid of candidate scales ($N=6$) and selecting candidates, rather than predicting an intrinsic scale end-to-end.

Cross-distribution transfer limitations: While scalar affine adapters generalize better than full-rank adapters across datasets, cross-domain transfer between SAE latents and Wikipedia topic vectors remains limited (e.g., GemmaScope-trained adapters achieve minimal transfer to Wikipedia retrieval in Table 12).

Mixed gains on detection scoring: At the 8B scale, trained adapters match but do not significantly outperform original auto-interpretability baselines on detection F1 (0.722 vs. 0.722 in Table 2), with the primary quantitative advantages manifesting in generation scoring hit rates.

Restriction to single-token embedding injection: The method injects activations exclusively into a single placeholder token position at layer 0; investigating multi-token soft prompts or intermediate layer injections remains largely unaddressed.
